newsitem.title: ALBANIA: West failed to heed signs of trouble in Albania.
newsitem.headline: West failed to heed signs of trouble in Albania.

text.p: The writing was on the wall a year ago.

Some would argue that the seeds of trouble in Albania took root earlier, at a time when the West was battling to end the war in Bosnia and had little appetite for getting bogged down in another Balkan state.

Moments after polls closed in the first round of a general election on May 26 last year, state-run television announced a landslide victory for President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party -- a startlingly accurate call in a country where communications are at best primitive.
The Democrats ended up with 122 deputies in a 140-seat parliament. International observers cried foul.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) produced what last year's chairman, Switzerland, called the body's worst election report, citing examples of voter intimidation, ballot stuffing and many other irregularities.

The United States urged Berisha to call new elections immediately, but Europe failed to press home the point with one voice. The Democrats felt able to snub Washington and advised the opposition to accept the handful of seats it had won.
The disorganised opposition Socialist Party decided political confrontation was the only way forward.
As a successor to the communists who ruled Albania for 45 years, it had failed to win many friends in the West by not shaking off some of the vestiges of its past quickly enough.

European states issued their standard expressions of concern as the long summer holidays beckoned and then, rightly, busied themselves in September with making sure Bosnia's first post-war elections went ahead as planned.

Asked if Europe made a mistake in believing that the Albania problem would go away, one senior Western diplomat said: "I tend to believe that human action can change the course of history. Some things could have been avoided."
What no one predicted was that the growing crisis would explode into the worst bout of violence in the region since Bosnia's warriors reluctantly laid down their arms in 1995.
Seething underneath the political instability, pyramid investment schemes were getting out of control.

The schemes, offering hugely attractive rates of return, began growing in 1994 to fill a void in a banking system which remained in embryonic form because of endless arguments between the Democrats, Socialists and other opposition parties.

The schemes began collapsing late last year and thousands of Europe's poorest people lost their cash. Albanians grumbled about the outcome of the 1996 election, but they took to the streets when they realised their nest eggs had disappeared overnight.

An armed rebellion swept the south in March and many towns are still outside government control. Organised "Citizens' Committees" are in charge in some towns but others are in the sway of armed gangs and mafia groups.
The international community is now pinning its hopes on a new general election on Sunday, but few politicians have come up with any feasible idea of how to restore order in the south.
A 7,000-strong international force has a mandate from the U.N. Security Council to protect aid, not to disarm rebels.
Some diplomats, who now insist a long-term plan to anchor democracy and a working economy is needed, had failed to detect signs of growing authoritarianism.

Berisha failed in a 1994 referendum to increase his powers but his party brought in a law a year later to ban former communist officials from standing for office, sweeping away most of Berisha's rivals, like Socialist leader Fatos Nano.
The same year, Albania was admitted to the Council of Europe, an organisation which promotes democracy.
After last year's controversial election, Albania was admitted to the Central European Initiative and was still receiving U.S. military aid.
"We have to learn the lessons of the past and that is what we are doing," a European diplomat said. "We hope that the best we can do is avoid another crisis in this country."
While diplomats agreed Albania had much to do to secure democracy, some acknowledged that the West had a long way to go in knowing how to deal with Europe's most volatile region.
